The seven vowel system (a, ɛ, ɔ, e, o, i, u) obtains for this position only, and in some languages of the group, although not in li-Duma or li-Wanji, the final vowel is reduced or even dropped in connected speech and in isolation. Relative length is also a relevant cue to stress placement. In Figure 2 (a), compare for example prefixal [u] in the initial syllable and radical [u] in the stem -lumi : the latter is longer by approximately one half (106 vs 70 ms).
new_statements.citation: Puech, Gilbert. 1990. Upstep in a Bantu Tone Language. Pholia 5: 175-186. CRLS, Université Lumière Lyon 2.
new_statements.locator: sec. 4 'Phonetic evidence', pp. 180-181 (scan pp. 4 of 7 in the copy we hold; retyped edition lines 5296-5303)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: rendered the 2-up scan we hold (7 A4 landscape pages, no text layer) and read scan page 4 (= printed pp. 180-181, sec. 4 'Phonetic evidence'). The reported passage is there verbatim, from 'First, it may be noticed that in B50 Bantu (and more generally in West Bantu languages), the radical vowel (i.e. the first vowel of the stem) is stressed' through '(106 vs 70 ms)'; the scan shows the IPA letters (a, ɛ, ɔ, e, o, i, u) exactly as the report quotes them (the retyped Pholia_N-5 text file renders them as E/O, so the report followed the scan, correctly). Page 181 also confirms the follow-up sentences used in rule_in_words: 'overall increase in the total duration of insistent forms,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Duma is a two-tone language (H/L, with High-tone copying, downstep and a semantically conditioned upstep). Word stress is on the radical (stem-initial) vowel, i.e. the first vowel after the noun-class or verbal prefix; it is cued by duration and by the fact that the full seven-vowel contrast is restricted to that position. Under emphasis (the 'insistent' upstep forms) duration increases on the initial (prefix) and final syllables rather than on the stressed radical.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The older Duma-specific grammar (Reeb 1895, p. 2) gives a syllable-counting formulation instead: stress on the penult in words of two and three syllables and on the antepenult in longer words, stronger or weaker 'suivant l'expression donnée au discours'; for the canonical prefix + CVCV or prefix + CVCVCV word this coincides with the stem-initial syllable, but the two formulations differ for other shapes.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: nominal forms (prefix + stem) in isolation and in the presentative construction; the group-level wording ('in B50 Bantu') is made in a paper whose data are li-Duma (Lastoursville) and li-Wanji, and the duration example is a li-Wanji token, so the Duma application is by the author's inclusion of li-Duma in the claim, not a Duma-specific measurement.
new_statements.identity_note: Puech 1990 describes 'li-Duma' spoken around Lastoursville (= Duma proper, duma1253) alongside 'li-Wanji' (= Wandji/Liwanzi, wand1266, Guthrie B501), which he treats as two dialects of one language; the stress sentence is phrased for B50 Bantu as a group, and the duration measurement is on a li-Wanji token. Reeb 1895 describes 'douma' of the Haut-Ogowé mission at Lastourville, i.e. the same variety.

sources.note: pp. 180-181 (sec. 4 Phonetic evidence): in B50 Bantu the radical vowel (first vowel of the stem) is stressed; the 7-vowel contrast holds only there; relative length is a cue (radical [u] 106 ms vs prefixal [u] 70 ms in li-Wanji mu-lumi); two lexical tones H/L with High-tone copying, downstep and a semantically conditioned upstep; li-Duma differs from li-Wanji in that only the radical vowel may bear an upstepped High. Scan pages 180-181 checked against the text: verbatim.

sources.note: Ch. I 'De l'Alphabet', principle 8, p. 2 (PDF p. 10; page image checked): 'L'accent, plus ou moins fort, suivant l'expression donnée au discours, se trouve pour les mots de deux et trois syllabes sur la pénultième; pour les mots de plus de trois syllabes il est placé sur l'antépénultième.' No tone marking anywhere in the grammar; 'voyelles accentuées' (p. 3) and 'consonnes accentuées' (p. 5) concern diacritics, not stress.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.2 'Liduma (B 51)', pp. 46-53: second-hand phonological sketch after Mouélé 1997 (7 short + 7 long vowels, consonants, 6 tonal realisations reduced to 2 tonemes H/B with allotony, syllable types V/CV/SV/CSV/NCV). No word-stress statement. Pp. 271-272: group-level speculation that B50 keeps the H/L contrast only in stem position T1, read as 'une évolution vers un processus accentuel' (citing Philippson 1991, Dodo-Bounguendza 2010).
